blogs.title: Only the Commissioner Can Penaltize? Minnesota’s Payment of Wages Act Interpreted
blogs.description: An in‑depth look at how the Eleventh Circuit read §§ 181.101(a) and 181.171 of Minnesota’s Payment of Wages Act as giving exclusive penalty‑enforcement authority to the state commissioner. The post compares this construction with other Minnesota statutes that expressly allow employees to recover civil penalties, surveys prior case law, and discusses what the decision means for workers who want direct punitive relief against employers.

blogs.title: Federal Standing Meets State Wage Penalties — The MFLSA Conundrum
blogs.description: This article unpacks the Eighth Circuit’s handling of Cohen’s claim for statutory penalties under the Minnesota Fair Labor Standards Act—a remedy payable to the commissioner rather than to the employee. It explores the standing analysis drawn from Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, mootness considerations when an employer halts illegal conduct, and why the court vacated summary judgment and remanded on jurisdictional grounds. The piece also looks at how other states structure similar penalty schemes and what plaintiffs can do to preserve a viable claim.

blogs.title: Stipulating Away Your Claims? The Perils of ‘All Wages Paid’ Agreements in Wage Litigation
blogs.description: A practical guide examining how Cohen’s settlement‑type stipulation—that he had been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages—shaped the district court’s summary‑judgment ruling while leaving open contentious penalty issues. The post discusses strategic drafting tips for employers and plaintiff counsel when using stipulations in wage‑class actions, including whether to reserve rights to statutory penalties or injunctive relief and how such reservations affect later motions.

blogs.title: Missed Injunctions: Why Cohen’s Request to Void an Overtime Policy Fell Flat
blogs.description: A procedural critique focusing on why Cohen’s attempt to obtain an injunction rescinding Consilio’s overtime policy was rejected. It explains how his shift in requested relief—from specific forms outlined in the complaint to a blanket policy reversal introduced only in briefing—violated Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a). The article offers guidance for plaintiffs on preserving injunctive claims through proper pleadings or timely motion practice before a case reaches summary judgment.
